paper_title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first 1 requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). Data are captured with handheld LiDAR scanner and head-mounted multi-camera recorder, without robots or motion-capture infrastructure; processing pipeline reconstructs meshes and 3D Gaussian splatting models, estimates camera trajectories and hand and body motion, generates hierarchical language annotations, and supports registration of recordings to scene geometry. The reconstructions serve as reference for benchmarks on depth and geometry estimation, 3D object detection, and spatial reasoning. We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors. 1. Introduction Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations [63, 50]. On the 42-task RoboDojo benchmark [8], GPT-6 Astra attains reported average success rate of 22.48%, surpassing the 40 public policies in that comparison [63], and it reaches 92% on RxR [23] instruction following and 82% on HM3D [45] object search [16]. These models nevertheless remain far from practical deployment: an evaluation across eight robot configurations reports no success in 11 pluginsertion trials across three platforms and 9 successes in 23 navigation-and-search trials for GPT-6 Astra, while tracking progress across many subtasks remains difficult [49]. Enabling large foundation models to control robots reliably over long-horizon, complex tasks in real environments requires two complementary resources: (i) behavior demonstrations from which the models can learn, and (ii) environments in which they can execute tasks and accumulate experience. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws relating performance to data, model size, and compute [18]; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors. Answering it first requires identifying which environment and behavior data to scale, and how such data can be produced and reused continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, dataset of real environments and behaviors for physical AI. Ropedia Xperience 2 combines LiDAR scans of real scenes with egocentric recordings of human activity; our registration pipeline can place the corresponding scene geometry, video, camera trajectories, and hand and body motion in common metric frame. Registered recordings can support human-to-robot motion retargeting, while scanned scenes can be converted into interactive simulation environments; registration checks and perscene quality control provide tools for auditing, filtering, and reusing the data. With Ropedia Xperience 2, we aim to establish gold standard for next-generation physical AI data collection and to lay the data foundation for scaling laws of physical AI over environments and behaviors. Ropedia Xperience 2 is collected with two-stage protocol that requires single operator and no robot or motion-capture infrastructure on site. Each scene is first scanned once with handheld 3D scanner, and its assigned tasks are then recorded with the HOMIE head-mounted 2 Figure 2 From composite-scene modalities to robot data. The released scan component contains 1,589 scenes. The broader collection inventory spans 596 locations and 4,230 task recordings totaling 131 hours. An automated pipeline produces scene meshes and 3D Gaussian representations, alongside camera trajectories, depth, hand and body motion, and hierarchical language captions. Ropedia Xperience 2 extends Xperience-10M [47], which provides about 10 million egocentric interaction clips totaling 10,000 hours, with metric scene scans and pipeline for registering egocentric recordings to them. To assess the fidelity of the data, we use the scan reconstructions as reference geometry in three benchmarks: depth and geometry estimation, 3D object detection, and spatial reasoning. These benchmarks evaluate existing models across diverse real-world scenes. Each capture is further reused to scale both environments and behaviors for robot learning (Figure 2). Here, environments are real spaces with their layouts and object relations, and behaviors comprise the recorded human task executions as well as the robot motions and interactions derived from them. We demonstrate four routes: Real-to-sim conversion turns single scan of real-world environment into an interactive digital twin that preserves the original layout and appearance, incorporates realistic physical properties, and supports part-level object interaction, yielding reusable environments for policy and control learning. Human-robot retargeting converts the recorded human behaviors, including long-horizon activities, into robot demonstrations from the estimated body and hand motion, without on-site robot deployment. Virtual teleoperation lets operators collect robot demonstrations in the converted simulation scenes, without physical robots and with automatic scene resets. Figure 3 Overview of data collection. (a) Before capture, each scene (Level 1) is assigned set of tasks (Level 2). (b) The scene is scanned once with the 3D scanner, with overlapping coverage, revisits, detail views, and high and low viewpoints. (c) Its tasks are then recorded individually with HOMIE; each recording begins before the task and ends after it, and the saved file is verified. One scene scan provides the environmental context for multiple task recordings. Rooms, tasks, viewpoints, and device views are illustrative. Long-horizon trajectory generation rolls out robots on new multi-step tasks in the converted simulation scenes, chaining navigation and manipulation across subtasks from varied start states and object configurations; more trajectories require only additional compute. Real-to-sim conversion scales environments, while retargeting, virtual teleoperation, and trajectory generation scale robot behaviors. Capture thus scales with operators rather than robots, and the captured data can be expanded into robot data without further on-site collection. These routes complement real-robot teleoperation by offering lower-cost paths to training environments and demonstrations at different levels of fidelity. 2. Data Collection Our goal is to capture natural human activity together with the 3D structure of the environment in which it occurs, providing spatial context for understanding how people interact with their surroundings. Scene collections such as ScanNet++ and DL3DV-10K emphasize multi-view observations of real environments [61, 30], while Ego4D and Nymeria capture egocentric activity and motion [17, 32]. Holi-World organizes human-egocentric experience into grounded learning resources [27], and SpatialBench evaluates spatial foundation models across scene domains and input densities [42]. UMI further demonstrates portable human-demonstration capture without requiring robot at the collection site [10]. We collect Ropedia Xperience 2 in real, in-use environments, including homes, restaurants, stores, offices, and outdoor sites. Collection is organized by scene: each scene (Level 1) is assigned set of tasks (Level 2) before capture (Figure 3a). Capturing environmental geometry and natural activity requires different sensing configurations. Scene scanning benefits from freely chosen viewpoints to observe high, low, and partially occluded regions, while activity recording requires both hands to remain free and the cameras to follow the operators viewpoint. We therefore use two complementary devices  (Table 1)  . The 3D scanner is handheld LiDAR device equipped with two fisheye and two wide-angle cameras, allowing the operator to scan the scene from varied viewpoints. HOMIE is head-mounted 4 egocentric recorder with four global-shutter fisheye cameras, two facing forward and two facing backward. The forward pair captures the hands and manipulated objects, while the global shutters avoid rolling-shutter distortion during rapid head motion. HOMIE also records inertial measurements and four-channel audio. For each scene, the operator first performs 3D scan and then wears HOMIE to complete the assigned tasks one by one (Figure 3). The protocol is designed to associate task recordings with 3D scan of the same scene, linking activity to its physical environment; Section 3.3 describes how they can be spatially registered. Scenes and Tasks The collection inventory contains 74 Level 2 tasks, 31 of which take place in work and retail scenes such as restaurants, stores, and offices (Figure 4a). By leading verb, the tasks fall into seven actions, which form five categories: pick and place, cleaning, rearrangement, folding, and inspection (Figure 4b). Placing or taking out objects (25 tasks), wiping and cleaning (23), and arranging and tidying (18) account for most tasks. The 4,230 uploaded recordings, each one execution of task, are concentrated in home scenes: placing, taking out, and folding dominate in bedrooms, and wiping in living rooms and bathrooms (Figure 4c). 2.2. Capture Protocol We standardize collection with written protocol so that captures are consistent across sites and operators. It covers scene preparation, 3D scanning, and HOMIE task recording; the latter two are shown in Figure 3b and c. Scene preparation. The scene must remain static from the start of the 3D scan until task recording begins. Before capture, we therefore minimize appearance changes and transient content: screens are turned off or set to static image, lights are turned on and kept constant, bystanders and pets leave the scene, and windows and other transparent surfaces are covered where possible. 3D scanning. Scanning aims for complete coverage with redundant views. The operator walks slowly through the scene, traversing each route in both directions, scans occluded and detailed regions at close range, and sweeps the device vertically to add high and low viewpoints. HOMIE task recording. Task recording aims to capture each activity completely and naturally. Before each recording, the operator checks that the device is secure and that no lens is obstructed. Recording begins before the task starts and ends after it is completed, so that each recording contains the entire activity. 5 Figure 4 Tasks by scene and action in the collection inventory. These assets share one coordinate frame, which we call the scene frame; because the geometry is measured by LiDAR, the scene frame is metric. The posed images and the mesh serve as the reference for registering the task recordings of the scene (Section 3.3), and the 3DGS model renders the scene from arbitrary viewpoints, such as the recorded HOMIE camera poses (Figure 5). 3.2. HOMIE Processing We use the same automated pipeline to process HOMIE recordings. Synchronization and calibration. The four cameras are hardware-synchronized, and all sensor samples are timestamped by the device clock. We place the four videos on common 30 fps frame index and link the IMU and audio samples to it by timestamp. Each device is calibrated 7 before capture, and every recording stores the intrinsics of the four fisheye cameras and their extrinsics relative to the IMU (Appendix B.1). Device trajectory and depth. The two forward-facing views are rectified into pinhole stereo pair, on which SLAM, depth, and hand estimation operate. SLAM estimates 6-DoF device pose for every frame and sparse landmark map in gravity-aligned metric frame whose origin is the head position at the first frame. stereo module additionally estimates metric depth with per-pixel confidence. Hand pose. Hands are represented with MANO [46] and estimated with our in-house annotation pipeline. The pipeline fits MANO to hand keypoints recovered from the calibrated stereo views, using cross-view reprojection consistency to refine the estimates. The output is 21 joints per hand in the stereo-left camera frame. When hand is outside the view or occluded, no estimate is produced for that frame. Body motion estimation. We estimate the wearers full-body motion with EgoAllo [62], using the SLAM-derived head trajectory as conditioning and our hand estimates as guidance. The motion is represented with SMPL-H [46], with body shape held constant within each recording. The output comprises 52 body and finger joints at 30 Hz in the recordings SLAM frame. The estimated motion is constrained by the observed head and hands, while unobserved body parts, particularly the legs, are inferred using the learned motion prior. Hierarchical activity annotations. We use large multimodal model to generate hierarchical activity annotations from the recordings. The annotations describe the recorded activity at three temporal scales. For the full recording, they summarize the main task and provide an overall activity description. Within the recording, they identify sub-tasks and actions with associated time intervals. For each sampled frame, they describe visible objects and their states, the state of each hand, and ongoing handobject interactions. All annotations are associated with the video timeline. The temporally localized actions are distinct from the task-level action categories in Section 2.1. Registration can then transform the device trajectory and estimated hand and body poses into the scene frame (Section 3.3), while the activity annotations remain associated with their corresponding timestamps. 3.3. ScanHOMIE Registration The scan reconstruction and each HOMIE recording are expressed in separate coordinate frames. To place human activity in its spatial context, we register the recordings device trajectory and estimated hand and body motion to the scene frame. As illustrated in Figure 5, this brings the egocentric observations, estimated motion, and scene geometry into shared spatial reference. Connecting egocentric activity to scene geometry is also central to EPIC Fields, which augments activity videos with reconstructed camera information [53]. We localize stereo-left frames in the scan using SIFT [31] matching, RANSAC [15], and PnP against scan image keypoints lifted onto the mesh, then fit the recording-to-scene transform by robust Umeyama alignment [54] of the corresponding camera centers. The transform allows small scale correction when supported by the trajectory and validation; otherwise, it is rigid. Held-out frames, IMU gravity consistency, and an ICP [4] check of stereo depth against the mesh are used to assess the alignment and assign PASS, WEAK, or FAIL labels (Appendix B.3). single transform cannot correct local SLAM drift within recording. 8 Table 3 Released scans and collection inventory. Scene QC and Release Decisions The upload inventory contains 1,780 works. Of the 1,610 completed scans with release grade or Delete decision, 1,589 (98.7%) are retained and 21 (1.3%) are Delete (Figure 6). These three grades sum to the released set and are the denominator for release-composition percentages; Delete remains outside the release. Grades follow the current QC records and release-policy overrides described in Appendix B.4. The 507 Reuse scans include partial coverage and other reconstruction defects. Home interiors account for 1,389 scans (87.4%), and bedrooms and living rooms together for 61.4% of the release. Among home categories, kitchens (81.6%) and bathrooms (58.0%) have the highest Reuse shares, against 31.9% overall. Applications The applications comprise three benchmarks (depth and geometry, 3D object detection, and spatial intelligence) and downstream demonstrations. All three benchmarks use the same 20 scanned scenes, listed in Appendix D.1. 5.1. Benchmarking Existing Models 5.1.1. Depth and Geometry Understanding human activity in scene requires recovering the surrounding geometry and the observers motion. We evaluate how well existing models recover depth, camera trajectories, and scene surfaces from multi-view images, and how their performance changes with the number of input views. Models. The comparison follows SpatialBench [42], with models grouped into its optimizationbased, end-to-end feed-forward, online, chunk-wise, SLAM-based, and test-time-training categories  (Table 4)  . Metrics. All models are evaluated on the same 20 scenes under Sparse (5 frames), Medium (11100 frames), and Dense (335500 frames) settings. Table 4(a) reports depth AbsRel, RMSE, and 𝛿1.03; panel (b) reports pose AUC@30, trajectory ATE, Chamfer distance (CD), and surface F-score at 5 cm. The scan reconstructions provide the reference geometry and camera poses. Depth is median-scaled per scene, so its scores evaluate scale-normalized depth quality. Frame selection, alignment, and metric definitions are detailed in Appendix D.2. Results. No single model leads across all metrics. 𝜋3 achieves the lowest trajectory ATE and the highest surface F-score across all three input settings, while DA3-Giant achieves the highest pose AUC in the Medium and Dense settings. More input views do not consistently improve performance: CUT3Rs pose AUC decreases from 0.4103 to 0.0625 between Sparse and Dense, whereas DA3-Giants increases from 0.7540 to 0.8074. Dense inputs also expose memory limitations, with DUSt3R and MASt3R unable to complete evaluation. These results highlight differences in geometric accuracy and scalability that are not captured by depth scores alone. 5.1.2. 3D Object Detection Annotations. Annotators manually label the 20 evaluation scenes for this benchmark, marking the category and 3D box of each object in the scene frame; these labels are the ground truth. Models. The comparison covers three groups  (Table 5)  : end-to-end models that predict boxes from images or point clouds (SpatialLM [34], LLaVA-3D [64], SceneScript [2], Map-Det3D [60]), language fields embedded in 3DGS (M3 [67], LangSplat [44]), and Boxer [13], which lifts open-vocabulary 2D detections to 3D boxes. Each method is queried with the object categories present in the scene. Metrics. AP25 and AP50 are average precision at 3D IoU thresholds of 0.25 and 0.5; mIoU@0.25 is the mean 3D IoU of predictions matched to reference box at IoU 0.25. Query and box conventions are in Appendix D.2. Results. Boxer leads on all three metrics. The other methods stay below 7 AP25, and LLaVA-3D and SceneScript produce no box that reaches IoU 0.25. The demonstrations use metric, gravity-aligned scene geometry and the pipelines ability to register HOMIE recordings to the corresponding scenes. Real-to-Sim turns scene into 13 simulator scene, in which an operator can teleoperate robot live (virtual teleoperation) and robot can run new multi-step tasks (long-horizon generation); retargeting drives robot with recorded human motion. Real-to-Sim Neural scene representations such as NeRF [35] support novel-view rendering, while Habitat 2.0 and BEHAVIOR-1K provide environments for physics-based robot interaction [51, 26]. Checks: joint velocity and torque within 90% of their limits, ZMP inside the support polygon, no scene or self-collision, and head and fingertip tracking error. Long-Horizon Trajectory Generation SayCan and PaLM-E explore language-conditioned task planning [1, 14], while Code as Policies generates robot policy programs from language [28]. MimicGen studies expanding demonstration datasets by adapting human demonstrations to new contexts [33]. Input: an object-level simulator scene from Real-to-Sim, robot model, and task given as sequence of subtasks. Output: robot trajectories that chain navigation and manipulation through every subtask, from varied initial robot and object poses. Checks: per-subtask and 16 full-task success from the simulators object states, task rules on the objects (nothing tipped or dropped, appliances and doors left as each subtask requires), trajectory duration, and generation yield and time per valid trajectory. We generate trajectories for one eight-subtask task in converted home environment: wheeled dual-arm robot picks up mug from the kitchen counter, opens the microwave, puts the mug inside, closes the door to heat it, takes it out, closes the microwave again, pushes the closed bedroom door open, and sets the mug on the bedside table (Figure 11). Each subtask is policy program that acts through whole-body controller and observes objects only through perception, not through the simulator state; the eight run in one continuous rollout without resets. Limitations The released scan component is dominated by home interiors and includes Reuse scans with partial coverage or other reconstruction defects. Release grades incorporate policy overrides and resolution of conflicting QC labels; they should not be interpreted as uniform visual or geometric validation of all retained scans. Separate scans may depict the same physical space, and the collection-site inventory is not verified site census of the released subset. The recording count and duration describe the collection inventory. Hand and body motion are estimated rather than motion-capture ground truth, unobserved body parts are inferred, and activity captions are model-generated. single recording-to-scene transform cannot correct local SLAM drift. 7. Conclusion Ropedia Xperience 2 extends Xperience-10Ms focus on human behavior with metric scans of real environments and pipeline for placing egocentric recordings and estimated motion in shared scene frame. Its two-stage collection protocol captures environments and behaviors without requiring robots on site. The resulting scene representations support three benchmarks for evaluating existing models, while real-to-sim conversion, human-robot retargeting, virtual teleoperation, and long-horizon trajectory generation demonstrate how captured scenes and recordings can be reused to produce simulation environments and robot trajectories. This reuse allows real capture to support both the study of observed human activity and the generation of further robot experience. We propose joint capture, spatial registration, and reuse of environments and behaviors as gold standard for physical AI data collection. These resources provide data foundation for studying scaling laws that relate physical AI capability to the scale and diversity of environments and behaviors. Synchronization, Calibration, and Coordinate Frames The four HOMIE cameras are hardware-synchronized to within 50 µs. Video, audio, and IMU samples are timestamped in nanoseconds on the device clock, and every frame-indexed output of the pipeline shares one 30 fps frame index; the IMU (200 Hz) is linked to this index through keyframe indices. Each device is calibrated before capture, with reprojection error below 0.5 px on the 1920 1088 camera images, and every recording stores the calibration of the device that recorded it: the intrinsics of the four fisheye cameras, the transform from the device body (IMU) frame to the first camera, and the chain of transforms between consecutive cameras. The two forward-facing fisheye cameras are rectified into pinhole stereo pair of 1920 1088 pixels, of which 1452 824 crop without black borders is used; stereo depth is stored at 480 272. Transforms use homogeneous column vectors, and T𝐴𝐵 maps point from frame 𝐵 to frame 𝐴. The SLAM world frame of recording is gravity-aligned with +𝑧 up, in meters, with its origin at the head position of the first frame; device poses map the body (IMU) frame to this world frame. Hand joints are expressed in the rectified stereo-left camera frame (OpenCV convention), and body joints in the SLAM world frame. After registration (Appendix B.3), the scene frame of the 3D scan replaces the SLAM world frame for all three. B.2. Pose and Language Annotation Hands. For each hand and frame, our in-house annotation pipeline provides 21 3D joints, the wrist pose, the finger-joint rotations, and the MANO shape coefficients, all in the rectified stereo-left camera frame. Frames in which hand is not estimated are marked as missing. Body. The body estimate comprises 52 SMPL-H joints covering the body and fingers, the local joint rotations, the root and head poses in the SLAM world frame, shape coefficients that are constant over the recording, and soft contact scores. Whenever hand is observed, the wrist and finger joints of the body agree with its MANO estimate. Language. We use large multimodal model to generate hierarchical language annotations for each recording. These annotations summarize the overall task, identify temporally localized subtasks and actions, and describe objects, hand states, and handobject interactions. B.3. We select well-textured stereo-left frames spread over the recording and match each against the scan images with SIFT features, scoring candidate images by the inliers of fundamental matrix estimated with RANSAC. QC notes identify defects such as moving people, door motion, invalid traversal, double imaging, failed reconstruction, and partial coverage. Release grades combine the recorded QC result with the release policy below; the checklist is not claim that every retained scan passes every check. The approved release retains only completed uploads assigned Perfect, Usable, or Reuse, counting each work once. Previous Delete decisions in Living room, Multi-room, Office, Meeting room, Store, Restaurant, Outdoor corridor, and Urban street are reassigned to Reuse. Completed scans without an explicit QC result are retained as Usable only in Living room, Multi-room, Outdoor corridor, Urban street, and Parking lot. This rule accounts for 7 scans in the QC registry and 84 additional scans documented in the release supplement. For conflicting recorded grades, the release takes the best in the order Perfect, Usable, Reuse, Delete; 33 retained scans use this rule. Delete decisions remaining after these rules are outside the release.
